summaries.example: Imagine a very long checklist. In ordinary logic, the checklist has only finitely many items. In an infinitary language, it might say: “Rule 1 is true, and Rule 2 is true, and Rule 3 is true...” continuing through infinitely many rules. This lets the language describe things that ordinary first-order logic cannot describe so precisely.
summaries.summary: Infinitary logic studies formal languages whose formulas may contain infinite conjunctions, disjunctions, and sometimes strings of quantifiers. A language is written L(κ,λ): roughly, it allows combinations shorter than κ and quantifier strings shorter than λ. The ordinary first-order language is the special case L(ω,ω), where formulas are finite. One important example, L(ω₁,ω), allows countably infinite lists joined by “and” or “or,” while keeping quantifier strings finite. Such languages can describe the standard natural numbers, all finite sets, and other classes that first-order logic cannot characterize in the same way. However, they often lose familiar properties. Compactness says that if every suitably small part of a set of sentences has a model, then the whole set has a model; this can fail for infinitary languages. Completeness, the existence of a reliable connection between truth and formal proofs, also becomes limited in many cases. The entry explains why finite-quantifier languages behave better, why infinite-quantifier languages resemble second-order logic, how large cardinals enter the compactness question, and how Barwise’s theorem gives compactness for carefully chosen sublanguages.
key_ideas: Ordinary first-order logic uses finite formulas, but infinitary logic permits certain infinite formulas.
Longer formulas can describe some patterns that ordinary logic cannot describe.
More expressive power can bring difficulties: many infinitary languages do not have the useful completeness and compactness features of first-order logic.
The language L(ω₁,ω) allows countably infinite conjunctions and disjunctions but only finite strings of quantifiers.
Special sublanguages based on admissible sets can recover a useful form of compactness.
summaries.why_it_matters: Infinitary logic shows that changing the rules for making formulas changes what mathematics can describe and what proof methods can guarantee. It helps explain the balance between expressive power and dependable reasoning. The subject also connects logic with set theory, model theory, and the study of mathematical structures.

important_terms.definition: A formal language that allows some lists of statements, choices, or quantifiers to have infinitely many members.
A way of joining statements with “and.” An infinitary conjunction can join infinitely many statements.
A statement that is true in a particular mathematical structure, such as a system containing numbers and operations.
A structure that makes all the sentences in a collection true.

questions_to_think_about: Would an infinitely long checklist ever be easier to use than many short checklists?
Why might a language that can say more also be harder to prove things in?
What could go wrong if every small part of a collection works, but the whole collection does not?

summaries.example: Consider a structure with a relation symbol <. In L(ω₁,ω), one can form the infinite formula x₀ < x₁ and x₁ < x₂ and x₂ < x₃, continuing through all natural-number stages. This formula uses a countably infinite conjunction but only finitely many quantifiers at a time. By contrast, L(ω₁,ω₁) can use an infinite quantifier sequence, allowing statements about every member of a countable sequence at once. That extra quantifier strength helps characterize well-orderings, but it also makes the language behave more like second-order logic and undermines completeness.
summaries.summary: Infinitary logic extends first-order logic by allowing formulas to contain conjunctions and disjunctions of infinite length, and in some languages quantifier sequences of infinite length as well. The notation L(κ,λ) records these limits: combinations have size less than κ, while quantifier sequences have length less than λ. L(ω,ω) is ordinary first-order logic. L(ω₁,ω) is especially important because it allows countably infinite combinations but only finite quantifier strings. It retains an effective completeness theorem for suitable countable-length deductions, and it supports results such as Scott’s theorem for countable structures. Yet it fails ordinary compactness: an uncountable collection of sentences can have every countable subcollection satisfiable while the whole collection has no model. Infinite-quantifier languages such as L(ω₁,ω₁) are stronger still. They can express ideas, such as properties of well-orderings, that cannot be captured by finite-quantifier languages, but their valid sentences are not definable in the relevant coding structure, yielding a form of incompleteness. The entry also studies generalized compactness and its relation to large cardinals. Finally, it explains how admissible sets provide closed sublanguages in which Barwise’s compactness theorem holds for appropriately definable collections of sentences.
key_ideas: L(ω,ω) is ordinary first-order logic; L(ω₁,ω) permits countably infinite conjunctions and disjunctions while retaining finite quantifier strings.
Infinitary languages have greater expressive power: L(ω₁,ω) can characterize the standard model of arithmetic and the class of finite sets.
Completeness can survive for L(ω₁,ω) with an appropriate countable-length deduction system, but compactness fails for arbitrary sets of premises.
Languages with infinite quantifier strings resemble second-order logic and are generally incomplete in a strong definability sense.
Questions about generalized compactness are linked to large-cardinal properties such as weak compactness and inaccessibility.
Barwise compactness restores a useful result for sublanguages associated with countable admissible sets and suitably definable sets of sentences.
summaries.why_it_matters: The subject tests a central logical trade-off: stronger languages can distinguish more structures, but their semantics and proof theory may become less manageable. Infinitary logic also reveals that compactness is not merely a technical convenience; it is tied to deep set-theoretic assumptions. The Barwise theorem shows that careful restrictions can preserve useful reasoning without returning all the way to ordinary first-order logic.

important_terms.definition: A formal language obtained from a first-order language by allowing conjunctions, disjunctions, and possibly quantifier sequences of specified infinite lengths.
The language L(κ,λ), which permits conjunctions and disjunctions of size less than κ and quantifier strings of length less than λ.
The property that every logically valid sentence can be obtained by an appropriate formal deduction system; first-order logic has this property.
The property that if every sufficiently small part of a set of sentences has a model, then the entire set has a model.
A formal expression that has no free variables and can therefore be true or false in a structure.
A structure in which a sentence, or every sentence in a set, is true.
A cardinal κ for which an appropriate infinitary language satisfies a corresponding compactness condition; such cardinals must be extremely large when uncountable.
A carefully closed collection of sets that supports restricted forms of recursion and proof construction; it is used in Barwise’s compactness theorem.

questions_to_think_about: Is greater expressive power worth losing a theorem such as compactness?
Why does allowing infinite quantifier strings make a language more like second-order logic?
How does the failure of compactness differ from the failure of completeness?
Why might restricting attention to a well-chosen sublanguage improve the behavior of infinitary logic?

summaries.example: Suppose a teacher wants to describe a class containing exactly the finite collections of objects. An ordinary first-order sentence cannot simply say “the collection has 0 objects, or 1 object, or 2 objects...” for every natural number, because that would require an infinite list. In L(ω₁,ω), an infinite disjunction can make that description in one sentence. The language becomes more powerful, but it also loses some guarantees that ordinary logic provides.
summaries.summary: Infinitary logic expands ordinary first-order logic by allowing some formulas to be infinitely long. The notation L(κ,λ) describes the permitted sizes: conjunctions and disjunctions have length less than κ, while strings of quantifiers have length less than λ. The familiar first-order case is L(ω,ω). In L(ω₁,ω), a formula may contain a countably infinite “and” or “or,” but quantifiers still come in finite strings. This extra space lets the language express important ideas that first-order logic cannot express in the same way. For example, it can characterize the standard model of arithmetic and the class of finite sets. However, the extra power creates costs. Compactness, which says that compatible small pieces guarantee a compatible whole, fails for general sets of infinitary sentences. Completeness can hold for L(ω₁,ω) under a suitable deduction system, but languages with infinite quantifier strings generally show a stronger failure of completeness and resemble second-order logic. The entry also examines generalized compactness, which depends on properties of very large cardinals, and Barwise’s compactness theorem, which works for certain sublanguages built from admissible sets.
key_ideas: First-order logic uses finite formulas; infinitary logic permits selected infinite constructions.
L(ω₁,ω) can describe the standard natural numbers and all finite sets in ways first-order logic cannot.
More expressive languages do not automatically preserve compactness or completeness.
Finite-quantifier languages generally behave better than languages with infinite quantifier strings.
The compactness question connects logic with very large infinite numbers called cardinals.
Barwise’s theorem gives a useful compactness result for certain carefully chosen sublanguages.
summaries.why_it_matters: Infinitary logic helps us see that the rules of a language shape both its descriptive power and its proof methods. It is useful for studying mathematical structures that ordinary logic cannot separate. At the same time, it shows why logicians value compactness and completeness: these principles make reasoning predictable, and they may disappear when a language is made more powerful.

important_terms.definition: A logic whose formulas may contain certain infinite lists of statements or quantifiers.
A formula made by joining statements with “and.” In an infinitary language, the joined list may be infinite.
A formula made by joining statements with “or.” An infinitary disjunction may offer infinitely many alternatives.
A mathematical structure in which a sentence or group of sentences is true.
A result saying that if all small enough parts of a collection of sentences have models, then the whole collection has a model.
A result connecting all true logical consequences with what can be produced by formal rules of proof.
A language allowing infinite conjunctions or disjunctions but only finite strings of quantifiers, such as L(ω₁,ω).
A special set used to build a well-behaved sublanguage for Barwise’s version of compactness.

questions_to_think_about: What kinds of patterns can an infinite “and” or “or” describe?
Why might a language become harder to control when it can say more?
Can every collection whose small parts work be expected to work as a whole?
Why would logicians study a restricted sublanguage instead of using the biggest possible language?
